puzzles.title: Development Policy & Interventions
puzzles.blurb: Test your grasp of real-world development policies and the evidence behind them.

questions.q: What is the key difference between a conditional and an unconditional cash transfer?
options: Conditional transfers require recipients to meet behaviours like school attendance
Unconditional transfers are always larger in value
Conditional transfers are only paid to men
questions.explanation: Conditional cash transfers (e.g. Brazil's Bolsa Família, Mexico's PROGRESA/Oportunidades) tie payments to behaviours such as keeping children in school or attending health check-ups. Unconditional transfers impose no such requirements.

questions.q: India's MGNREGA primarily guarantees rural households:
options: Up to 100 days of paid wage employment per year
questions.explanation: The Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act guarantees up to 100 days of wage employment per rural household per financial year, acting as a self-targeting safety net.

questions.q: A common critique of microfinance from rigorous evaluations is that it:
options: Always lifts borrowers out of poverty within a year
Has modest average effects on income and rarely transforms livelihoods on its own
Is illegal in most developing countries
questions.explanation: Randomised evaluations (e.g. by Banerjee, Duflo and colleagues) generally find microcredit expands business activity modestly but does not, on average, dramatically raise income or consumption.

questions.q: M-Pesa, frequently cited in development economics, is an example of:
options: A mobile money / digital payments platform
questions.explanation: M-Pesa is Kenya's mobile-money system. Studies suggest it improved financial resilience and helped households smooth consumption against shocks.

questions.q: 'Import substitution industrialisation' (ISI) refers to a strategy of:
options: Exporting raw commodities to rich countries
Replacing imported manufactured goods with domestic production behind protective barriers
Removing all tariffs to maximise free trade
questions.explanation: ISI, prominent in mid-20th-century Latin America and India, used tariffs and subsidies to build domestic industry in place of imports. It later drew criticism for inefficiency and lack of competitiveness.

questions.q: The 'graduation approach' for the ultra-poor typically combines:
options: An asset transfer, consumption support, training and coaching over a fixed period
questions.explanation: Pioneered by BRAC and tested across multiple countries, the graduation model bundles a productive asset, short-term consumption support, savings, training and regular coaching to move households onto sustainable livelihoods.

questions.q: Which measure best captures multidimensional poverty?
options: An index combining deprivations in health, education and living standards
questions.explanation: The Multidimensional Poverty Index (MPI), developed by OPHI and UNDP, counts overlapping deprivations across health, education and living standards rather than relying on income alone.

questions.q: A randomised controlled trial (RCT) in development economics is valued mainly because it:
options: Creates a credible counterfactual by random assignment, isolating a programme's causal effect
Guarantees a programme will scale nationally
Removes the need for ethics review
questions.explanation: Random assignment makes treatment and control groups comparable on average, so differences in outcomes can be attributed to the intervention. RCTs still face questions of cost, ethics and external validity.

puzzles.title: Drivers of Inequality
puzzles.blurb: What widens the gap — and what narrows it?

questions.q: A Gini coefficient of 0 represents:
questions.explanation: The Gini ranges from 0 (everyone has identical income) to 1 (one person has everything). Most countries fall roughly between 0.25 and 0.60.

questions.q: 'Skill-biased technological change' tends to:
options: Compress wages between skilled and unskilled workers
Raise demand and pay for higher-skilled workers relative to others
questions.explanation: When technology complements skilled labour, it raises the relative demand and wages of skilled workers, widening wage inequality unless education keeps pace.

questions.q: The Palma ratio focuses attention on:
options: The top 10% relative to the bottom 40%
questions.explanation: Gabriel Palma observed the middle's share is fairly stable, so the action is at the ends. The Palma ratio divides the richest 10%'s share by the poorest 40%'s share.

questions.q: Which policy is most directly aimed at inequality of opportunity?
options: Universal access to quality early education
questions.explanation: Equalising access to quality education early in life targets the roots of unequal outcomes rather than only redistributing after the fact.

questions.q: Wealth inequality is typically ____ income inequality.
questions.explanation: Because wealth accumulates and is inherited, its distribution is almost always more concentrated than the distribution of annual income.

questions.q: Intergenerational mobility is low when:
options: A child's outcomes are largely independent of their parents'
A child's outcomes are strongly predicted by their parents' position
questions.explanation: Low mobility means your parents' rung on the ladder strongly predicts your own — opportunity is 'sticky' across generations.

questions.q: Horizontal inequality refers to disparities:
options: Between culturally or identity-defined groups (e.g. caste, ethnicity, region)
Within a single household over time
questions.explanation: Frances Stewart's concept of horizontal inequality captures systematic gaps between groups, which are strongly linked to grievance and conflict.

puzzles.title: Applying Gender Analysis
puzzles.blurb: From theory to practice: doing gender analysis in programmes.

questions.q: 'Practical gender needs' differ from 'strategic gender interests' in that practical needs:
options: Challenge the existing division of power
Address immediate conditions without transforming gender relations
questions.explanation: Maxine Molyneux's distinction: practical needs (e.g. clean water, childcare) ease daily burdens; strategic interests (e.g. legal rights, decision-making power) aim to transform unequal relations.

questions.q: Gender mainstreaming means:
options: Running a one-off project for women
Assessing implications for all genders in every policy and programme
questions.explanation: Adopted at the 1995 Beijing conference, mainstreaming makes gender concerns integral to the design, implementation and evaluation of all interventions.

questions.q: A 'gender-blind' programme is one that:
options: Ignores gender roles and so often reinforces existing inequalities
questions.explanation: Gender-blind design assumes interventions affect everyone equally; in practice it usually entrenches the status quo by overlooking differential roles, needs and power.

questions.q: Intersectionality, as Kimberlé Crenshaw framed it, highlights that:
options: Gender is the only axis of inequality
Overlapping identities (e.g. gender, race, caste, class) produce distinct, compounded experiences
Class always matters more than gender
questions.explanation: Crenshaw showed that, for example, Black women's experiences cannot be understood by analysing race or gender alone — the axes intersect to create unique forms of disadvantage.

questions.q: 'Unpaid care work' is significant for gender analysis because it:
options: Is evenly shared between men and women everywhere
Falls disproportionately on women and is invisible in GDP, constraining their other opportunities
Is fully counted in national accounts
questions.explanation: Care work — cooking, cleaning, childcare, eldercare — is overwhelmingly done by women, uncounted in GDP, and limits time available for paid work, education or leisure ('time poverty').

questions.q: Engaging men and boys in gender programming is generally seen as:
options: Important, because transforming norms requires the participation of those who hold power
A replacement for working with women
questions.explanation: Sustainable change in gender norms requires engaging men and boys as allies and stakeholders — not as a substitute for, but as a complement to, women's empowerment.

questions.q: Sex-disaggregated data refers to data that is:
options: Broken down and reported separately by sex/gender
questions.explanation: Disaggregating by sex reveals gaps that pooled averages hide, and is a first step toward gender-responsive monitoring.

questions.q: The WID, WAD and GAD approaches differ chiefly in that GAD:
options: Focuses only on adding women to existing projects
Analyses gender relations and power, not just women in isolation
questions.explanation: Women in Development (WID) added women to projects; Women and Development (WAD) stressed their role; Gender and Development (GAD) shifted to relations of power between genders and structural change.

puzzles.title: Data Feminism & Algorithmic Justice
puzzles.blurb: Power, bias and justice in data systems.

questions.q: A central principle of 'Data Feminism' (D'Ignazio & Klein) is to:
options: Treat all data as perfectly objective
Examine and challenge power in how data is collected and used
Avoid collecting any data on gender
Maximise data collection regardless of consent
questions.explanation: Data Feminism asks who has power in data, whose interests it serves, and how to challenge unequal power — rejecting the myth of view-from-nowhere objectivity.

questions.q: The 'Gender Shades' project by Joy Buolamwini found that facial-recognition systems:
options: Had much higher error rates for darker-skinned women than for lighter-skinned men
Were unbiased once trained on more data
questions.explanation: Gender Shades exposed large accuracy gaps: commercial systems misclassified darker-skinned women far more often, revealing how unrepresentative training data encodes bias.

questions.q: 'Data colonialism' describes:
options: The appropriation of human life and behaviour as raw material for extraction and profit
questions.explanation: Couldry and Mejias coined the term for the way platforms treat human activity as a resource to be harvested, echoing historical colonial extraction.

questions.q: 'Missing data' matters for justice because:
options: It is always a harmless gap
Groups not counted are often rendered invisible to policy and resources
questions.explanation: What is not counted often does not count: undercounted groups (e.g. femicide, unpaid care, informal workers) become invisible in decisions that rely on data.

questions.q: A model can be 'accurate' overall yet unjust when:
options: It performs equally across all groups
Its errors fall disproportionately on already-marginalised groups
questions.explanation: Aggregate accuracy can hide disparate error rates. Fairness requires examining how harms and benefits are distributed across groups, not just the average.

questions.q: Counter-data practices involve:
options: Communities producing their own data to make injustices visible
questions.explanation: Counter-data — such as community-led counts of police violence or femicide — is generated by affected groups to surface what official systems omit.

questions.q: 'Proxy discrimination' occurs when an algorithm:
options: Explicitly uses a protected attribute like race
Uses a seemingly neutral variable that correlates with a protected attribute
questions.explanation: Even without using race or gender directly, a model can discriminate via correlated proxies (e.g. postal code, name), reproducing structural inequities.

puzzles.title: Designing M&E Systems
puzzles.blurb: Build M&E systems that are useful, not just compliant.

questions.q: A Theory of Change differs from a logframe mainly because it:
options: Explains why and how change is expected to happen, including assumptions and pathways
Is required by donors but never used
questions.explanation: A Theory of Change maps the causal pathways and assumptions from activities to impact; a logframe is a more structured summary often derived from it.

questions.q: In a results chain, 'outputs' are:
options: The direct products of activities (e.g. people trained, clinics built)
questions.explanation: Outputs are the immediate, largely controllable deliverables of activities. Outcomes are the behavioural or condition changes that follow; impact is the higher-level change.

questions.q: A good outcome indicator is primarily:
options: Specific, measurable and clearly tied to the result it tracks
Whatever data is easiest to collect
questions.explanation: SMART indicators are specific, measurable, achievable, relevant and time-bound, and should be selected to genuinely reflect the intended result — not just convenience.

questions.q: Why collect a baseline before implementation?
options: Without a 'before' measure, you cannot credibly show change over time
questions.explanation: A baseline establishes the starting point against which midline and endline values are compared, enabling assessment of change.

questions.q: 'Downward accountability' refers to being answerable to:
options: The communities and people a programme is meant to serve
questions.explanation: MEAL stresses accountability not just upward to donors but downward to affected communities, via feedback and complaints mechanisms.

questions.q: Adaptive management means:
options: Using monitoring data and learning to adjust the programme during implementation
questions.explanation: Adaptive management treats M&E as a feedback loop: evidence and reflection inform course corrections rather than just end-of-project judgement.

questions.q: The distinction between 'attribution' and 'contribution' matters because:
options: In complex settings it is often more credible to claim a contribution than sole attribution
questions.explanation: Attribution claims your programme caused the change; in messy real-world settings, contribution analysis more honestly assesses your programme's role alongside other factors.

questions.q: Utilization-focused evaluation is organised around:
options: The intended uses of intended users
questions.explanation: Michael Quinn Patton's approach designs evaluation backward from how primary intended users will actually use the findings.

puzzles.title: Research Ethics Fundamentals
puzzles.blurb: Principles and dilemmas in ethical research with people.

questions.q: The three core principles of the Belmont Report are:
options: Respect for persons, beneficence and justice
questions.explanation: The Belmont Report (1979) sets out respect for persons (autonomy and informed consent), beneficence (do good, minimise harm) and justice (fair distribution of risks and benefits).

questions.q: Informed consent requires that participants:
options: Sign a form regardless of understanding
Understand the study, participate voluntarily, and can withdraw without penalty
Be unaware they are in a study
questions.explanation: Valid consent means adequate information, comprehension, and genuinely voluntary agreement — plus the freedom to withdraw at any time.

questions.q: Offering very large payments to participants risks being:
options: Always ethical because it respects their time
Unduly coercive, pressuring people to accept risks they otherwise would not
questions.explanation: Reasonable compensation is appropriate, but excessive inducement can undermine voluntariness, especially among economically vulnerable participants.

questions.q: Confidentiality differs from anonymity in that anonymity means:
options: The researcher knows identities but keeps them secret
No identifying information is collected, so even the researcher cannot link data to a person
questions.explanation: Anonymity = identity is never recorded. Confidentiality = identity is known to the researcher but protected. They require different safeguards.

questions.q: An Institutional Review Board (IRB) / ethics committee primarily:
options: Reviews studies to protect participants' rights and welfare before they begin
questions.explanation: Ethics review boards assess risks, consent procedures and protections for participants — especially vulnerable groups — before approval.

questions.q: The Tuskegee Syphilis Study is a notorious example of:
options: Withholding available treatment and deceiving participants, causing lasting harm and mistrust
A randomised controlled trial done well
A study with full informed consent
questions.explanation: For decades, Black men with syphilis were left untreated without their informed consent even after penicillin became available — a key motivation for modern research-ethics rules.

questions.q: When researching a vulnerable population (e.g. children, refugees), researchers should:
options: Apply lower ethical standards for efficiency
Take additional protections proportionate to heightened risk and reduced power
Assume risks are the same as for any adult
questions.explanation: Heightened vulnerability calls for stronger safeguards: assent procedures, gatekeeper care, and special attention to power imbalances and potential harms.

questions.q: 'Do no harm' in field research includes:
options: Anticipating and minimising psychological, social, legal and economic risks to participants and communities
questions.explanation: Beneficence and non-maleficence extend beyond physical harm to reputational, emotional, legal and community-level risks — including how findings are shared.

puzzles.title: Epidemiology Essentials
puzzles.blurb: Understanding disease patterns and control.

questions.q: Incidence measures ____ while prevalence measures ____.
options: new cases over a period; existing cases at a point in time
questions.explanation: Incidence = rate of new cases over time; prevalence = the proportion of a population that has the condition at a given moment. A chronic disease can have high prevalence but low incidence.

questions.q: R0 (the basic reproduction number) represents:
options: The death rate of a disease
The average number of people one infected person infects in a fully susceptible population
questions.explanation: If R0 > 1 an outbreak tends to grow; if R0 < 1 it tends to die out. Interventions aim to push the effective reproduction number below 1.

questions.q: Herd immunity protects a community because:
options: Enough people are immune that the pathogen struggles to find susceptible hosts, indirectly protecting others
It eliminates the need for any vaccination
questions.explanation: When a sufficient share of the population is immune, chains of transmission break, indirectly protecting those who cannot be vaccinated.

questions.q: A screening test's 'sensitivity' is its ability to:
options: Correctly identify those who have the disease (true positives)
Correctly identify those without the disease
questions.explanation: Sensitivity = true-positive rate (catching real cases). Specificity = true-negative rate (correctly clearing the healthy). There is usually a trade-off between them.

questions.q: Which is an example of primary prevention?
options: Vaccination or sanitation that stops disease from occurring
Early screening to catch disease sooner
questions.explanation: Primary prevention stops disease before it starts (e.g. vaccines, clean water). Secondary = early detection/screening; tertiary = limiting damage from established disease.

questions.q: 'Social determinants of health' include:
options: Income, education, housing, and other conditions in which people are born, live and work
questions.explanation: Most health outcomes are shaped by upstream social and economic conditions far more than by clinical care alone.

questions.q: A case-control study works by:
options: Following healthy people forward in time
Comparing people with a disease (cases) to those without (controls) and looking back at exposures
questions.explanation: Case-control studies start from outcome status and look backward at exposure, which is efficient for rare diseases but vulnerable to recall and selection bias.

questions.q: Universal Health Coverage (UHC) means:
options: Free private insurance for the rich
All people can use needed health services without financial hardship
questions.explanation: UHC, a Sustainable Development Goal target, means everyone obtains the quality health services they need without being pushed into poverty by the cost.

puzzles.title: Climate Policy & Justice
puzzles.blurb: From the Paris Agreement to climate justice.

questions.q: The Paris Agreement's central goal is to hold global warming to:
options: Well below 2°C, pursuing efforts to limit it to 1.5°C, above pre-industrial levels
Whatever each country prefers, with no shared target
questions.explanation: Adopted in 2015, the Paris Agreement aims to keep warming well below 2°C and to pursue 1.5°C, implemented through countries' Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs).

questions.q: 'Mitigation' and 'adaptation' differ in that mitigation:
options: Helps communities cope with impacts already happening
Reduces the greenhouse gas emissions driving warming
Is only about building sea walls
questions.explanation: Mitigation tackles the cause (cutting emissions); adaptation manages the consequences (e.g. drought-resistant crops, flood defences). Both are needed.

questions.q: Carbon pricing via a cap-and-trade system works by:
options: Setting a total emissions cap and letting firms trade tradable allowances
questions.explanation: Cap-and-trade fixes the quantity of emissions (the cap) and lets the market set the price of allowances; a carbon tax instead fixes the price and lets quantity adjust.

questions.q: 'Common but differentiated responsibilities' (CBDR) holds that:
options: All countries must cut emissions by the same amount
Countries share responsibility but richer, higher-emitting nations should do more
Climate change is no one's responsibility
questions.explanation: CBDR recognises that wealthy industrialised nations contributed most historical emissions and have greater capacity, so they bear greater responsibility to act and to support poorer nations.

questions.q: The 'loss and damage' agenda concerns:
options: Support for harms from climate impacts that cannot be prevented by mitigation or adaptation
The cost of building wind farms
questions.explanation: Loss and damage addresses unavoidable impacts — such as land lost to sea-level rise — and the question of who pays, a key demand of vulnerable nations.

questions.q: A 'just transition' aims to ensure that moving away from fossil fuels:
options: Protects the livelihoods of workers and communities dependent on high-carbon industries
questions.explanation: A just transition seeks decent work and support for workers and communities (e.g. coal regions) so that decarbonisation does not deepen inequality.

questions.q: Climate vulnerability is generally highest among:
options: Low-income communities and countries that contributed least to emissions
Only coastal cities in rich countries
questions.explanation: Those who did least to cause the crisis — low-income communities, small island states, marginalised groups — often face the greatest exposure and the least capacity to adapt, the core of climate-justice arguments.

questions.q: Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs) are:
options: Legally binding identical targets set by the UN
Each country's self-defined climate pledges under the Paris Agreement
questions.explanation: Under Paris, each country sets and updates its own NDC; the agreement uses transparency and a 'ratchet' mechanism to encourage rising ambition over time.

puzzles.title: Reading Data Critically
puzzles.blurb: Practise interpreting everyday data claims.

questions.q: A rate rises from 2% to 4%. That is a 2 ____ increase but a 100% ____ increase.
questions.explanation: Going from 2% to 4% is +2 percentage points, but the relative change is (4-2)/2 = 100%. Confusing the two is a common way to mislead.

questions.q: 'Correlation does not imply causation' means:
options: A link between two variables doesn't prove one causes the other
questions.explanation: Variables can move together due to a third factor, reverse causation, or chance. Establishing causation needs more than correlation.

questions.q: A survey of 30 people reports a result with great confidence. The main concern is:
options: Small sample size means wide uncertainty
questions.explanation: Small samples produce large margins of error, so confident-sounding percentages may not be reliable.

questions.q: A bar chart's y-axis starts at 90, not 0. This can:
questions.explanation: Truncating the axis visually magnifies differences, a classic source of misleading charts.

questions.q: Cherry-picking data means:
options: Selecting only the figures that support your point
questions.explanation: Cherry-picking presents a biased slice of evidence by ignoring data that contradicts the claim.

puzzles.title: Rights & Duties Quiz
puzzles.blurb: Test your knowledge of fundamental rights and the structure of the Constitution.

questions.q: Which article is known as the 'heart and soul' of the Constitution per B.R. Ambedkar?
questions.explanation: Ambedkar called Article 32 — the right to constitutional remedies, which lets citizens approach the Supreme Court directly — the heart and soul of the Constitution.

questions.q: Directive Principles of State Policy differ from Fundamental Rights mainly because they are:
questions.explanation: DPSPs (Part IV) are non-justiciable guidelines for governance, whereas Fundamental Rights (Part III) can be enforced through the courts.

questions.q: The Right to Education was made a fundamental right by inserting:
questions.explanation: The 86th Amendment (2002) added Article 21A, making free and compulsory education for children aged 6–14 a fundamental right.

questions.q: The 'basic structure doctrine' was established in which landmark case?
questions.explanation: In Kesavananda Bharati (1973) the Supreme Court held that Parliament cannot amend the 'basic structure' of the Constitution.

questions.q: How many fundamental rights categories are currently in the Constitution?
questions.explanation: There are six categories of Fundamental Rights, after the Right to Property was removed as a fundamental right by the 44th Amendment.
